summary: Costa Rica grants visa-free stays of up to 180 days to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and many other countries, strictly expects proof of onward travel (airlines enforce it at check-in), and lets many visa-required nationals enter with a valid US, Canadian or Schengen visa instead of a Costa Rican consular visa.

fee.notes: Approximate fee — the consular visa stamp plus legal fees vary by consulate and nationality; confirm locally before applying. Restricted nationalities need extra authorisation from the Immigration Commission and wait longer.

passportValidity.text: Officially Costa Rica only requires your passport to be valid for the length of your intended stay (first-group nationalities technically need as little as one day beyond entry), but airlines often apply stricter checks — 3 to 6 months' validity is strongly recommended to avoid boarding problems.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate (ICVP) is required if you arrive from, or recently visited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — including much of South America (Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Venezuela, Bolivia) and sub-Saharan Africa. The vaccine must be administered at least 10 days before arrival. Not required for direct arrivals from North America or Europe.

source.name: Ministerio de Salud de Costa Rica

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is no longer an entry requirement (the COVID-era insurance mandate ended). Medical cover is still recommended — private hospitals are excellent but expensive.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería

onwardTicket.text: Proof of onward or return travel leaving Costa Rica within your permitted stay is a legal entry requirement — and airlines enforce it strictly at check-in, refusing boarding without it. A bus ticket out of the country also counts, but a confirmed flight is safest.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería

proofOfFunds.text: Officers may ask for proof of economic means — the commonly applied benchmark is about USD 100 per month of intended stay — though most tourists are never asked.

source.name: Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments of USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: Duty-free allowance: 500 g of tobacco and 5 litres of alcoholic beverages per adult.
Strict biosecurity rules apply to fresh fruit, plants, seeds and animal products — declare them or leave them at home.
The USD 29–31 airport departure tax is now included in virtually all airline tickets — you no longer pay it separately at the airport.

payments.text: Cards are accepted almost everywhere tourists go, and US dollars are accepted nearly universally (change comes in colones, often at a poor rate). Keep some colones in cash for sodas (small local restaurants), rural areas, buses and tips.

safety.text: Costa Rica is one of the safer countries in Central America, but petty theft is the main visitor risk — never leave belongings visible in a parked rental car or unattended on a beach. Rip currents cause more tourist deaths than crime; swim only at beaches with lifeguards or ask locally about conditions.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Costa Rica Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is the dry season ('verano') on the Pacific side — the most reliable weather for beaches and wildlife; the green season (May–November) is cheaper and lush, with mostly-sunny mornings and afternoon downpours.

tips.text: Book your exit before you fly — airlines strictly enforce Costa Rica's onward-ticket rule at check-in and will refuse boarding on a one-way itinerary without proof of onward travel.

Renting a car? Mandatory local liability insurance is added on top of quoted prices (budget for it), never leave anything in a parked car, and check whether your route needs 4x4 — some beach-town roads involve unbridged river crossings that rental contracts often exclude.
Rip currents are the leading cause of tourist deaths in Costa Rica — many popular beaches have no lifeguards. If caught, swim parallel to the shore until free of the current, then in.
Tap water is safe to drink in most of Costa Rica, including San José and the main tourist towns; in remote coastal or rural spots, ask locally or use bottled water.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Costa Rica?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Costa Rica visa-free for tourism and can be granted up to 180 days. You do need a passport valid for your stay and proof of onward travel — airlines check for the onward ticket before boarding.

faq.question: How long can tourists stay in Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Visa-free nationals of the first group (US, Canada, UK, EU, Japan and many more) can be granted up to 180 days. The immigration officer decides the exact number of days at entry — check the stamp in your passport, as it controls your legal stay.

faq.question: Can I enter Costa Rica with a US or Schengen visa instead of a Costa Rican visa?
faq.answer: Often yes. Nationals of visa-required countries who hold a valid multiple-entry visa or residence permit for the United States, Canada or the Schengen area can generally enter Costa Rica without a consular visa, for up to 30 days (or until the visa expires, if sooner). Confirm the current rules for your nationality with a Costa Rican consulate before booking.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Only if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — including Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Venezuela, Bolivia and much of sub-Saharan Africa. In that case you must show an ICVP certificate issued at least 10 days before arrival. Direct arrivals from North America or Europe need nothing.

faq.question: Do I have to pay a departure tax when leaving Costa Rica?
faq.answer: Almost never any more — the roughly USD 29 exit tax is bundled into virtually all international airline tickets. Only some charter or very old bookings still require paying it separately at the airport; land borders charge a small exit fee (about USD 8–10).
